extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing stand-up comedians; students, scholars, and general readers interested in comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating, performing, and evaluating live stand-up comedy: genres, joke structures, delivery techniques, show roles, audience interaction, common anti-patterns, and career/recording formats. Useful for performers preparing material or researchers studying the art form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and form of stand-up comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up comedy is an art form that involves a stand-up comic and an audience; the performer addresses the audience directly and delivers humorous and satirical monologues, typically composed of tightly crafted sets or acts and often including live crowd interaction (crowdwork).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances can include one-liners, stories, observations, or shticks and may employ props, music, impressions, dialects, magic tricks, or ventriloquism; venues include comedy clubs, festivals, bars, nightclubs, colleges, casino showrooms, or theaters. During constraints (e.g., pandemic) performers may use video conferencing or outdoor locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Intended to counter the established approach of set up/punchline in mainstream comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative (alt-) comedy deliberately departs from traditional joke structures and mainstream expectations; it's a stylistic choice affecting material and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytelling using exaggeration and humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal comedy emphasizes narrative and personal stories, often shaped for comedic effect through exaggeration and selection of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A fictional persona created by the performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The performer sustains a character throughout the set; character traits and consistency are key to believability and comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan (dry) delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate display of emotional neutrality or no emotion as a form of comedic delivery to contrast with the ridiculousness or absurdity of the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called dry humor or dry-wit; effectiveness depends on contrast between content and affect, and on precise timing and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressionist work
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating notable figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impressions rely on recognizable vocal and physical mannerisms; effectiveness depends on accuracy, novelty, and placement within a routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insult comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consists mainly of offensive insults, usually directed at the audience or other performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style trades on sharp barbs and audience complicity; it risks alienation and requires skill to remain entertaining rather than purely abrasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous songs or musical parodies, sometimes without lyrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses melody, rhythm and musical structure for comic effect; may be integrated with spoken material or performed as distinct bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation on the absurdities of everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational material often mocks 'normal' behaviors and relies on shared experience and recognition; it can inadvertently affirm narrow ideas of 'normal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule of people, institutions, or ideas through jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire aims to comment on or undermine targets, often with political or social intent; requires clarity of target and perspective to land effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Framed around a specific topic related to current events or dealing with issues that are important or popular at the current time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical material gains immediacy from relevance but may have limited longevity; requires up-to-date knowledge and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tends to involve use of tactics like puns, double entendres and rhymes to entertain audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery tends toward one-liners; wordplay requires linguistic precision and can be high-density in punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians make jokes at their own expense, often poking fun at their own flaws, insecurities, or embarrassing experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor comes from vulnerability and relatability, which can make the comedian more likable; balance is important to avoid undermining the performer's stage persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine construction (bits, interconnection, closer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics develop routines by constructing and refining jokes and interconnected 'bits' that form an interwoven narrative leading to the 'closer', the final joke that ties the show's themes together for a satisfying conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong routine builds thematic coherence and escalates toward a closer; bits should be tightened and arranged for narrative and comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core joke structure (premise, setup, punchline, topper/tagline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes are the juxtaposition of two incongruous things and are made up of the premise, set-up, and punchline, often adding a twist, topper, or tagline for an intensified or extra laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes often rely on surprise, misdirection, and compact language; adding toppers or taglines increases laugh density if timed well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and timing (intonation, inflection, attitude, timing, rule of three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery relies on the use of intonation, inflection, attitude, and timing as well as stylistic devices such as the rule of three, idioms, archetypes, or wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical delivery elements are central to turning written material into performed laughs; the rule of three and other devices structure expectations and subvert them for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraprosdokian as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: A surprising punchline that changes the context or meaning of the setup (paraprosdokian).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device depends on reinterpreting earlier material; the element of surprise is essential and must be set up carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jester's privilege (permission to mock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians can use the jester's privilege, the right to discuss and mock anything freely without being punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cultural notion is used to frame risky or transgressive material, but performers should still consider audience context and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up vs punching down (target selection guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept that comedy should 'punch up' at the rich and powerful without 'punching down' at those who are marginalized and less fortunate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative guide to target selection in jokes; the article notes debate and criticism about the terms themselves and urges awareness of socio-political identity and power dynamics when choosing targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke theft and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation and plagiarism are considered 'social crimes' by most stand-ups; accusations of joke theft occur, and those accused sometimes claim cryptomnesia or parallel thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is difficult to successfully sue for joke theft due to the idea–expression distinction; treating jokes as socially owned within the community underscores ethics and reputation management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience as co-constructor (audience contract and responsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up audiences 'are both co-constructors of the situation' and 'co-responsible for it' via an unspoken contract that allows exploration of unexpected, controversial, or scandalous subjects; reception hinges on the audience's understanding of the premise and appreciation of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled comics react instantly to audience reaction and use it to further the narrative; success depends on creating spontaneity, fostering intimacy, deterring heckling, and reading the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd work
rubrics_metrics.description: Talking directly with audience members through prewritten bits, improvisation or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd work engages the audience dynamically; it requires improvisational skill, quick thinking, and careful risk management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open mic purpose and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Open mic events are slots used by comedians to work on material or to show off skills to get an opener slot; may be booked or walk-in and are often bringer shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open mics are for testing new material and gaining stage experience; 'bringer shows' require performers to bring paying guests in exchange for stage time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opener, feature, and headliner roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical stand-up shows follow a structure where the host warms up the audience and introduces the opener, feature, and headliner; the host may also act as the opener in smaller shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles have conventional expectations (e.g., emcee warms up, opener plays shorter set); established comics earn regular bookings while jobbing comics may perform multiple venues in a day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festivals as career and discovery venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Festivals showcase up-and-coming acts; promoters and agents use festivals to seek out new talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing at festivals can increase exposure and provide networking opportunities with industry professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV specials and comedy albums (format and runtimes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced comics may produce television specials or comedy albums; a 'half-hour special' is typically between 20 and 35 minutes runtime excluding commercial breaks and an 'hour-long special' is typically between 40 and 65 minutes excluding commercial breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specials can be recorded on tour or at dedicated shows and may be distributed via TV, VOD, film, or audio formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tight five
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-minute routine that is well-rehearsed and consists of a comedian's best material that reliably gets laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'tight five' is often used for auditions and is a stepping stone to getting a paid spot; consistency and laugh reliability are key evaluation points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out (polishing process)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process in which brand new jokes are introduced and polished over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material improves through repeated performance and iteration; open mics and early shows are essential 'work out' settings for refining timing, wording, and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombing / Dying
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to get laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bombing indicates material or delivery isn't working for that audience; learning from failures is part of the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat
rubrics_metrics.description: A pause specifically to create comic timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-placed beats shape rhythm and expectation; overlong or mistimed pauses can undermine jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference to a joke earlier in the set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callbacks reward attentive audiences and build cohesion; they should be spaced and set up to maximize payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clapter
rubrics_metrics.description: When the audience cheers or applauds an opinion that they agree with, but which is not funny enough for them to laugh at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coined by Seth Meyers; clapter indicates agreement applause rather than genuine laughter and can be a signal about material that panders rather than lands comedically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chewing the scenery (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being overly theatrical or 'trying too hard' to get a laugh, especially when failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overacting is generally seen as a poor technique that draws attention to the performer rather than the joke; subtlety and authenticity are often preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpsing / breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: When the comedian laughs unintentionally during a portion of the show in which they are supposed to keep a straight face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corpsing can derail momentum; experienced performers learn strategies to recover or incorporate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hack (clichéd material)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clichéd or unskilled comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'hack' signals reliance on tired premises or crude technique; originality and craft are measures to avoid this label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mugging (cheap physicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulling silly faces to elicit a cheap laugh, often relying on exaggerated expressions and physical gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mugging generates cheap laughs but can be seen as a lack of substantive material; it may work sparingly but risks audience disengagement if overused.
